newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Standard Chartered Bank plans more Asia alliances.
newsitem.headline: Standard Chartered Bank plans more Asia alliances.

text.p: Standard Chartered Plc said on Wednesday it expects to expand dramatically across Asia over the next few years, capitalising on its existing infrastructure in many centres to tap into the region's high economic growth.

Chief executive officer Malcolm Williamson told Reuters his bank was discussing possible alliances in Asia with more than five European banks and hoped to be able to make an announcement about one of them in the next one or two months.
"We already have very big businesses in Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia but we are looking to expand quite dramatically in many of the other countries," Williamson said in an interview.
"Primarily, I'd highlight the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand as being particular markets that we are looking at very hard in Southeast Asia to see how we can expand."
Although Standard Chartered is based in London, 70 percent of its revenue, assets and profits come from Asia and the bank expects the region to provide the fastest area of future growth.
The bank's pretax profit rose to 870 million pounds (US$1.42 billion) in 1996, up from 661 million in 1995.
It has recently announced a series of alliances with non-Asian banks which it hopes will entrench its position as a dominant player in the Asian banking industry.
It formed joint ventures in Asia last year with Westpac Banking Corp, First Chicago NBD Corp and Massachusetts-based Fleet Financial Services.

Williamson said such alliances allowed Standard Chartered to offer use of its financial services in Asia to banks which did not have an Asian presence and, in turn, let it benefit from significent economies of scale.
"We have announced deals so far with a number of banks, four in North America and one in Australia and we are in the course of discussion with quite a number of other banks," he said.
"We haven't announced any in Europe yet but we are in quite detailed discussions with a number of people," he said.

"We have five deals up and running now and we've got considerably more than that under discussion. Just when they'll come to fruitition and when we will be able to announce them, I wouldn't like to predict...I hope within the next month or two."
Williamson said alliances with other banks offered potential gains for both sides.

"What we are saying to them is, 'Look we have a huge infrastructure in Asia, we are in every country except North Korea. You are not in Asia and its going to be expensive to get there if you want to. Why don't you use us as if we were a branch network extension?'," he said.
Williamson said he expected Standard Chartered's main area of growth to come from retail banking, but also predicted expansion in its corporate banking and treasury activities.
"We have a lot of traditional retail banking, credit cards and mortgages. We are looking to expand that in Southeast Asia," he said.

Williamson said the bank's investments in Asia could grow faster than the seven percent a year forecast for its global operations when the company's released its last full-year financial results in February.
"Across the region, we are probably investing 60 or 70 million pounds or more this year and I guess that number will probably have to increase as time goes by," he said.
